newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank of Canada seen on hold until Q3.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Canada seen on hold until Q3.

text.p: The Bank of Canada is not expected to hike interest rates until at least the third quarter of 1997, now that the U.S. Federal Reserve has decided to hold its rates steady, economists said on Wednesday.
Canada's central bank might hold off raising rates even longer if the Canadian dollar continues firming and the Fed remains on hold, the economists added.
"I don't think the bank is in any particular hurry to tighten and I think there is at this point little need for them to do so," said Tim O'Neill, chief economist with Bank of Montreal.

Speculation that the Bank of Canada would soon hike rates increased last week after Governor Gordon Thiessen said the bank had moved to a more neutral strategy on monetary policy from a stimulative one.

Thiessen's comments led many to believe that the bank would soon follow an increase in U.S. rates. A U.S. rate hike would likely weaken the Canadian dollar, which would loosen overall monetary conditions in Canada.
The Bank of Canada measures monetary conditions using both the level of interest rates and the currency. A weaker dollar is seen having the same impact on the economy as an interest rate cut.

But the Canadian dollar rallied sharply after the Fed held rates steady on Tuesday. Given the dollar's strength, there was little chance the Bank of Canada would now raise rates independent of the Fed, economists said.

"Obviously the external environment is a lot more friendly to the bank and that's showing up in the stronger currency. The strength in the currency has given them a significant amount of leeway," said Mark Chandler, senior economist with Goldman Sachs Canada.

Canadian inflation remains subdued and the economy carries a great deal of slack. In its semi-annual Monetary Policy Report released last week, the Bank of Canada calculated that the gap between actual production and the economy's capacity to produce was 2.5 percent at the end of 1996.

"The basic story line remains the same. There's lots of excess capacity. There's lots of unemployment. There's no price pressures," said Carl Weinberg, chief economist with High Frequency Economics. "I see no reason for the Bank to hike rates right now."
Weinberg said that given the slack in the economy, Canadian rates could remain at current levels for the next six to 12 months if the Canadian dollar continued to strengthen.

Analysts said, however, that a near-term rate increase by the Bank of Canada could not be ruled out completely. A sharp sell-off in the Canadian dollar would prompt the Bank of Canada to hike rates to rebalance monetary conditions.
But with the Fed's rate-setting Open Market Committee not scheduled to meet until July 1, the risk of a currency sell-off was seen as minimal.
"The only significant risk would be sharp currency weakness, but it just doesn't look like that would be likely to happen with the Fed on hold right now," said Goldman's Chandler.
